problem: Prior navigation systems either demand precise goals or instructions (image-goal topological methods like NoMaD/ViNT, VLN models, LIM2N's sketch+language interface) or use hand-coded rules (ROS NavStack). They break when a non-expert's sketched route is rough or wrong, for example passing through walls. They also cannot respect implicit scenario rules such as staying in lane, using crosswalks, or avoiding rocks in an orchard.
motivation: People give robots abstract, noisy guidance such as a rough sketch on a map or a short verbal goal, and expect them to fill the gaps with commonsense. Such behaviour is hard to write as a reward or a rule set, but humans demonstrate it easily. The paper therefore imitates human teleoperation with a pre-trained VLM, which already carries commonsense priors, and trains it on deliberately 'misleading' sketches so it learns to follow intent rather than the literal line.
key_idea: Fine-tune a VLM by imitation learning on human teleoperation demos to map a front-view RGB image, a 'canvas' map image (occupancy map + rough human sketch + the robot's own past trajectory) and a language instruction to K-means-discretized waypoint tokens. The demos include intentionally noisy sketches.
insight: Treating waypoint prediction as classification over 128 K-means waypoint tokens lets the VLM model multimodal action distributions; the paper states K=128 beat 32/64/256 empirically, no numbers given. Training on 31–51% deliberately misleading sketches is what lets CANVAS succeed where a literal path-follower (NavStack) cannot even be run. The VLM pre-training ablation (Table VI) shows pre-trained weights matter mainly for generalization: seen Office total SR 100 vs 93, but unseen Gallery 67 vs 50 and real office 63 vs 53. Two further observations: model scale is not decisive, since the 0.7B CANVAS-S matches or beats the 8B CANVAS-L in orchard, road IVR and real-world total SR. Camera-based perception learned from demos avoids small hazards like rocks, which caused 56% of NavStack failures with LiDAR height thresholds.
method: Canvas map input: the pre-extracted occupancy map is rendered as an image with the human sketch trajectory S and the robot's odometry-tracked hindsight trajectory H(t) overlaid. It is re-rendered every step as X_c(t) and serves as both the human–robot interface and the robot's memory.

VLM policy: Idefics2-style model. The vision encoder encodes the front-view image X_f(t) and canvas map X_c(t), a projector maps them to visual tokens, and the LLM consumes these plus the language instruction L. It autoregressively outputs 4 waypoint tokens [w0..w3].

Action tokenization: continuous waypoints are discretized into K=128 tokens via K-means clustering (RT-2/Hydra style). Navigation becomes classification, which handles multimodal action distributions.

Imitation learning: NLL loss over waypoint tokens on COMMAND human teleoperation demos. LoRA (r=256, alpha=512, dropout 0.1), AdamW with lr 2e-5 (LLM) and 5e-5 (projector/vision encoder), batch 32, 5 epochs.
Two model sizes: CANVAS-L keeps Idefics2-8B with pre-trained weights. CANVAS-S swaps in the SigLIP-L vision encoder and Qwen2-0.5B LLM (0.7B total) for on-robot deployment.

Execution: predicted discrete waypoint tokens are decoded to continuous waypoints and tracked by a PD controller producing (v, ω). In the real world, pose comes from FAST-LIO2 SLAM, with on-device inference on NVIDIA AGX Orin (≈400 ms S, ≈800 ms L).

COMMAND dataset: 3 Isaac Sim environments (office, street, orchard) built in Unreal Engine, with 3,343 human-annotated episodes (48 h, 219 km). Each has Precise or Misleading sketch instructions, language goals, commonsense constraints and teleop trajectories. New metrics are TDD (IQM Fréchet distance to the human trajectory, successes only) and IVR (human-judged constraint violations).

setting.backbone: CANVAS-L: Idefics2-8B (LoRA fine-tuned); CANVAS-S: SigLIP-L vision encoder + Qwen2-0.5B LLM in Idefics2-style architecture (LoRA fine-tuned)
setting.training_data: COMMAND train split: 3,343 human teleoperation demos with human-drawn sketch instructions (Office 2,263, Street-Road 403, Street-Sidewalk 410, Orchard 267), 48 h / 219 km of driving in NVIDIA Isaac Sim; 31–51% of sketches deliberately misleading. Simulation only; no real-world training data.
setting.observation: monocular front-view RGB + canvas map image (occupancy map with human sketch and odometry-based hindsight trajectory) + language instruction
setting.action_space: sequence of 4 waypoints, each one of 128 K-means-discretized waypoint tokens, tracked by a PD controller outputting continuous linear/angular velocity
setting.simulator: NVIDIA Isaac Sim (environments built in Unreal Engine)
setting.privileged: pre-extracted occupancy map of the environment (canvas map) and robot pose from odometry (FAST-LIO2 SLAM in real world); human sketch route is given as the instruction

numbers_note: The only benchmark is the paper's own COMMAND suite, not a standard VLN/ObjectNav benchmark. Each environment is a separate entry. 'SR' is the paper's 'Total SR' over Precise and Misleading sketches. SR/CR/IVR are percentages; TDD is in meters, computed on successes only. Test sets are tiny: 10 episodes per environment (20 for Street-Road), each run 3 times with random start orientation. Some printed rows have SR+CR>100 (e.g. Orchard CANVAS-S Precise SR 73%/CR 60%; Gallery CANVAS-L Precise SR 100%/CR 7%), although success is defined as reaching the goal without collision. They are copied as printed. The K=128 vs 32/64/256 token ablation is stated in text only, without numbers. Latency is 400 ms (S) / 800 ms (L) on AGX Orin. The NavStack baseline was not run on misleading sketches.
results: CANVAS matches the rule-based ROS NavStack on easy precise-sketch settings (Office, Street-Road) and clearly beats it on hard ones: Orchard precise SR 67–73% vs 0%, Sidewalk 87% vs 53%. It also handles misleading sketches, where NavStack cannot operate (Office total SR 100% for CANVAS-L, Orchard 67% total for CANVAS-S), with lower commonsense-violation rates. It generalizes to the unseen Gallery (67% total SR) and transfers zero-shot to a real office robot (69% total SR for CANVAS-S). VLM pre-training adds +17 pts total SR on the unseen environment and +10 pts in the real world.
limitations: Evaluation is on the authors' own small test sets (10–20 episodes per environment × 3 runs), with a single rule-based baseline that cannot use language or misleading sketches. There is no comparison to learned navigation or VLN methods such as NoMaD, LIM2N or NaVid.
Performance with misleading sketches drops sharply in unseen and real settings (33% misleading SR for CANVAS-L in Gallery and the real office). Sidewalk collision rates remain high.
It requires a pre-built occupancy map and accurate odometry/SLAM pose for the canvas map. On-device latency is 400–800 ms per step.
